Rivian Commercial Van (Source: Rivian)
Rivian has started delivering the first major hardware upgrade to its electric van since production began in 2021: a bigger LFP battery pack good for 30% more range, and a new dual-motor AWD version.
The company confirmed in its Q3 2026 shareholder presentation that deliveries of the new variants began in early October. That’s the first real spec bump for a van that has been stuck at about 160 miles of rated range for years.
A 129 kWh pack and a dual-motor option
Rivian first mentioned the upgrade in its Q4 2025 letter, which we covered in February when Amazon’s fleet of Rivian vans grew 50%. At the time, Rivian only said it was “developing” a larger battery and AWD to “expand EDV route coverage” in Amazon’s network.
Now it’s shipping. In today’s presentation, Rivian says the new variants are “specifically designed to expand route coverage into more rural networks,” with the AWD configuration and the bigger pack offering “a 30% increase in range.”
Advertisement - scroll for more content
EPA certification documents for the 2027 EDV 700, issued September 17, list the new pack at 129 kWh usable. Rivian has marketed the current van with a 100 kWh LFP pack, so that’s roughly 29% more energy, which lines up with the 30% range claim.
The upgrade is limited to the bigger 700 van, the one with 652 cubic feet of cargo space. The smaller 500 keeps its existing pack and front-wheel drive.
What it means for range
The EPA filing gives unadjusted lab range figures, which always run high because they skip the correction for real-world driving:
Current EDV 700 (FWD): 261.7 miles
New EDV 700 FWD: 355.5 miles (+36%)
New EDV 700 AWD: 322.25 miles (+23%)
Rivian rates the current 700 at “up to 160 miles.” Apply Rivian’s 30% to that and the new FWD van lands around 208 miles. Using the AWD van’s smaller 23% gain from the EPA tests, we estimate the dual-motor version at about 195 to 200 miles.
So AWD costs roughly a third of the range gain. For a van, that’s a fine trade. Rural routes mean longer distances between stops, plus gravel, mud, and snow, which is exactly where a front-wheel-drive van with a full load of packages in the back struggles.
200 miles is roughly what Rivian promised for the van when deliveries to Amazon started in 2022, before the rated figure settled closer to 160 miles. Rivian is finally there, four years later.
Rivian needs fleet customers beyond Amazon
The timing helps on the sales side too. Rivian’s van business is still overwhelmingly Amazon, years after the exclusivity period ended in late 2023. We spotted a Rivian van in Walmart+ livery on a car hauler in Indiana just this week, though neither company has announced a deal.
The competition has also thinned out. GM ended BrightDrop van production in Ontario and Canoo went bankrupt, leaving Ford’s E-Transit as the main full-size electric alternative in the US.
Electrek’s Take
This is the upgrade the van needed. 160 miles was always fine for dense urban Amazon routes, but it boxed Rivian out of a big chunk of the fleet market: rural delivery, utilities, telecom, anyone who can’t guarantee a short loop and an overnight charge.
Getting to around 200 miles real-world, with AWD as an option, opens a lot of those routes. And unlike most of the EV van market right now, Rivian is actually building and improving its product rather than killing it.
The question is whether Rivian can turn that into customers other than Amazon. A Walmart+ wrap on a car hauler is a nice sign. We’d want to see a real order. If you’re running a fleet and these specs change your math, we’d love to hear from you.

Covenant Logistics Group reported a 19.2% year-over-year increase in third-quarter revenue Thursday, driven by strong growth in its managed freight segment .
The Chattanooga, Tennessee-based carrier (NYSE: CVLG ) generated $353.9 million in total revenue for the quarter ended Sept. 30, compared with $296.9 million a year earlier.
Freight revenue excluding fuel surcharges rose 17.2% to $315.1 million from $268.8 million.
Other highlights during the quarter included improved freight pricing , even as the trucking company continued shrinking its tractor fleet and shifting capacity toward long-term contracts.
Net income increased to $10.7 million, or 40 cents per diluted share, compared with $9.1 million, or 35 cents per share, in the third quarter of 2025.
On an adjusted basis, Covenant earned 50 cents per diluted share, up 13.6% from 44 cents a year earlier.
Chairman and CEO David R. Parker said the results marked the first time since the second quarter of 2022 that adjusted earnings per share increased both sequentially and year over year.
“We were pleased with our third-quarter earnings of $0.40 per diluted share, or $0.50 per diluted share on a non-GAAP adjusted basis,” Parker said in a news release .
The company’s operating income increased to $12.5 million from $7.9 million a year earlier. However, its adjusted operating ratio deteriorated to 95% from 94.4%, reflecting continued pressure from operating expenses.
Covenant will hold a conference call to discuss results with analysts at 10 a.m. Friday.
Covenant Logistics Q3 2026 financial and operating performance
Metric | Q3 2026 | Q3 2025 | YoY change
Total revenue | $353.9M | $296.9M | +19.2%
Truckload total revenue | $204.6M | $199.7M | +2.5%
Freight revenue excluding fuel (companywide) | $315.1M | $268.8M | +17.2%
Truckload revenue per total mile* | $3.03 | $2.53 | +19.8%
Truckload revenue per tractor per week* | $5,778 | $5,445 | +6.1%
Managed Freight revenue | $121.6M | $72.2M | +68.4%
Managed Freight adjusted operating income | $7.08M | $3.04M | +133.3%
Expedited freight revenue excluding fuel | $70.6M | $80.2M | -12.0%
Expedited adjusted operating income | $4.16M | $5.14M | -19.0%
Adjusted earnings per share | $0.50 | $0.44 | +13.6%
Covenant Logistics Group key third quarter performance indicators.
Managed Freight drives revenue growth
Covenant’s Managed Freight segment was the primary driver of the company’s third-quarter revenue growth, generating $121.6 million compared with $72.2 million in the same period last year, an increase of 68.4%.
Adjusted segment operating income more than doubled to $7.1 million from $3 million, while its adjusted operating ratio improved to 94.2% from 95.8%.
The company attributed the gains primarily to the integration of brokerage operations acquired during the fourth quarter of 2025, along with customer rate increases and lower purchased transportation costs.
Parker said the acquired brokerage operations delivered their strongest quarterly performance since joining Covenant.
The company’s existing brokerage business also benefited from sourcing additional carrier capacity to handle overflow expedited freight.
Covenant cautioned that sourcing qualified carrier capacity at prices below contractual freight rates remains challenging as trucking capacity exits the market. Rising insurance and claims expenses also pose risks to Managed Freight profitability.
Truckload fleet shrinks as revenue per mile climbs
Covenant’s combined Truckload operations generated $204.6 million in total revenue, up 2.5% from $199.7 million a year earlier.
However, Truckload freight revenue excluding fuel surcharges declined 3.4% to $166 million from $171.8 million.
The decline was largely attributable to an 8.9% reduction in the company’s average tractor fleet, which fell to 2,186 tractors from 2,400 a year earlier.
Despite operating fewer trucks, Covenant reported improved pricing and revenue productivity.
Average freight revenue per total mile climbed 19.8% to $3.03 from $2.53, while average freight revenue per tractor per week increased 6.1% to $5,778 from $5,445.
Average miles per tractor during the quarter declined 11.4% to 25,081 from 28,306.
President Paul Bunn said higher rates and an improved freight mix helped offset the impact of operating fewer tractors.
However, inflation and costs associated with repositioning equipment and drivers weighed on profitability.
Truckload adjusted operating income declined to $7.9 million from $10 million, while the segment’s adjusted operating ratio deteriorated to 95.3% from 94.2%.
Bunn said truckload operating expenses increased approximately 20.8% year over year on an adjusted basis, compared with a roughly 19.7% increase in freight revenue per total mile.
The company cited rising wages, employee benefits, equipment depreciation, maintenance and technology costs, along with temporary expenses related to starting new customer contracts.
Expedited revenue falls as Dedicated business expands
Covenant’s Expedited segment continued transitioning toward multiyear capacity agreements.
Expedited freight revenue excluding fuel surcharges declined 12% to $70.6 million from $80.2 million a year earlier.
The segment’s average tractor fleet fell 21.4% to 677 units from 861, while adjusted operating income declined 19% to $4.2 million.
Despite the reduction in fleet size, average freight revenue per tractor per week increased 12% to $7,934.
By the end of September, approximately 58% of Covenant’s Expedited tractors were operating under committed capacity agreements, compared with about 40% at the end of the second quarter.
Dedicated freight revenue excluding fuel surcharges increased 4.2% to $95.4 million from $91.6 million.
Dedicated revenue per tractor per week climbed 6.2% to $4,810, supported by expansion in the company’s agricultural protein-related transportation business and its decision to exit less profitable dedicated contracts.
Across its entire asset-based fleet, Covenant said approximately 80% of tractors were operating under long-term contracts at the end of the quarter.
Parker said the company’s longer-term goal is to place substantially all of its asset-based business under dedicated or other committed freight contracts by the end of the current freight market upcycle.
Freight demand holds steady, but costs remain elevated
Parker described freight demand as adequate across most sectors and strong in certain markets tied to U.S. economic growth.
However, he said tightening driver capacity and inflation continue to create significant operating challenges.
“Driver capacity is tight, and the cost of recruiting, retaining, and compensating drivers is increasing significantly,” Parker said.
He added that higher expenses for wages, equipment ownership, maintenance and technology have largely offset the benefits of freight rate increases.
Covenant expects its transition toward committed capacity contracts to reduce earnings volatility and improve profitability as the freight market strengthens.
The company’s Warehousing segment also faced profitability challenges during the quarter.
Warehousing freight revenue increased 7.8% to $26.7 million, but adjusted operating income declined to $888,000 from approximately $2 million a year earlier.
The company attributed the decline to operational inefficiencies at new customer locations and labor inflation.
Covenant forecasts further earnings improvement
Covenant expects a modest sequential increase in earnings per share during the fourth quarter as it continues shifting equipment into higher- margin committed contracts and reduces repositioning expenses.
The company also anticipates growth in its Dedicated fleet and a stable Expedited fleet, with a greater percentage of tractors operating under long-term agreements.
Its 49% ownership stake in Transport Enterprise Leasing contributed $5.7 million in pretax income during the quarter, compared with $3.6 million a year earlier. Covenant expects a lower contribution from the leasing business in the fourth quarter.
As of Sept. 30, Covenant reported approximately $283.9 million in net indebtedness, down $12.4 million from the end of 2025.
The company also reported $75.2 million in immediately available borrowing capacity under its asset-based lending facility.
For the remainder of 2026, Covenant expects net capital equipment expenditures of $35 million to $40 million.
Why it matters: Covenant’s earnings improvement highlights how trucking companies are using higher contract rates, smaller fleets and asset-light brokerage operations to offset persistent cost inflation and uneven freight demand.

1972 Challenger High School Driver Sat 25 Years, Gets New Owner and Engine, Drops Massive Burnouts
83 photos
Photo: YouTube/Dylan McCool
Rescuing a classic American muscle car after decades of slumber requires equal parts mechanical ingenuity, patience, and a healthy dose of stubbornness-infused faith. That’s all it takes, apparently, to make an engineless 1972 Dodge Challenger run and drive from Alabama to Tennessee. Parked inside a barn for 25 years and missing its engine for over 20 years, the Mopar icon proves miracles are real. And perfectly within the grasp of reason.
The story of this 1972 Dodge Challenger began in 1989, when previous owner Eddie Ball purchased the coupe while attending high school. Inspired by his aunt, who owned a triple-black 1972 Challenger rally car powered by a 340 cubic-inch engine that he could not acquire, Ball searched for his own example. An acquaintance soon directed him to this baby blue Challenger in Anderson, Alabama, fulfilling a dream – and setting in motion a chain of events that ended on Dylan McCool’s YouTube channel.
When Ball bought the Dodge, it was a dependable daily driver equipped with a 318 cubic-inch V8, an automatic transmission, and functional air conditioning. He drove the car throughout high school and took it on his senior trip to Panama City, Florida. Roughly two years later, he installed a 1969 model 340 small-block and mounted 4-speed manual pedals, though tight finances and impending fatherhood kept the automatic transmission in place.
The Challenger saw regular road duty until around 2001 or 2002, when another motorist pulled out in front of Ball, damaging the passenger-side front fender and header panel. Forced off the road, the coupe retreated into storage. Having met Troy McCool (Dylan’s father) at regional car shows, Ball traded vehicles and parts with him for years. Over 20 years ago, Ball sold the 340 engine, fuel tank, and fuel lines to Troy.
Photo: YouTube/Dylan McCool Troy McCool installed that small-block motor into a 1970 Dodge Challenger, which he eventually sold to a friend who still owns the vehicle today. Meanwhile, Ball kept the engineless 1972 shell tucked indoors. With four grandchildren and a fifth grandchild on the way, shifting family priorities finally convinced Ball to pass the torch. He sold the Challenger to Dylan McCool, bringing the Mopar family history full circle after 25 years.
Despite sitting stationary for most of this millennium, the Challenger preserved its structural integrity remarkably well. The body retained much of its factory baby blue paint, complemented by a green replacement passenger fender, a primered Rally hood replacing the original flat hood, earlier 1970 or 1971 bumpers, and a rear ducktail spoiler from a Challenger T/A. Inside, Ball had converted the originally blue cabin to black using pristine original seats from yet another donor car.
Beneath the dust, the Dodge boasted rock-solid floor pans, clean frame rails, and only minimal corrosion on a rear quarter panel. Even without an engine under the hood, the chassis offered an enviable foundation for a revival. It still carried a rebuilt front suspension, a refreshed automatic transmission with an aftermarket loose-stall torque converter, long-tube headers feeding a 3-inch dual exhaust with Flowmaster mufflers, and an 8.75-inch rear axle housing.
Photo: YouTube/Dylan McCool To return the pony Dodge to the pavement, Dylan arrived with a trusted 360 cubic-inch small-block V8 that he had previously installed in his 1972 Dodge Dart Swinger in 2013. Built with a stock rotating assembly, stock cylinder heads, an air-gap intake manifold, and a mild Comp Cams XE268 camshaft, the engine required an externally balanced B&M flexplate torqued to 55 foot-pounds before being hoisted into the bay.
The YouTuber and his trusty sidekick, Briar, replaced the front transmission seal and wrestled the 360 V8 between the long-tube headers. After bolting on an Edelbrock carburetor, modifying the kickdown linkage, and correcting a Mallory Unilite distributor that was initially set 180 degrees out of phase, they fired the engine. The V8 roared to life with 50 pounds of oil pressure, expelling a quarter-century’s worth of mouse nests out the tail pipes. A literal shove scoop, as you can see in the video.
Rebuilding the fuel and cooling systems brought unexpected comedy when Dylan McCool realized the brand-new replacement gas tank had flown out of his pickup bed during the one-hour drive to the shop. Troy McCool drove to Stephens Performance for another new tank, while Dylan hand-bent a 3/8-inch aluminum fuel line and fitted a universal $150 eBay radiator.
Photo: YouTube/Dylan McCool Tapping the top of the bellhousing with a hammer resolved minor flexplate rubbing. It’s called “wrenching,” but it’s not really serious unless there’s a bit of hammering sprinkled into the fix.
Getting the Challenger to stop safely required two days of persistent labor in chilly weather. The pair installed a new master cylinder, a front brake caliper, two rear wheel cylinders inside the 10-inch drums, and fresh rubber brake hoses after heating seized fittings with a torch. Mounted on factory police steel wheels with dog-dish hubcaps, the coupe rolled into the sunlight with Eddie Ball happily behind the wheel once more, for one last dance.
Photo: YouTube/Dylan McCool After pressure-washing 25 years of grime off the baby blue body and securing the broken headlight panel, Dylan and Briar ventured out into 35-degree weather for a shakedown run. Although the dead vacuum booster demanded heavy leg effort on the brake pedal, the car halted reliably. Initially stuck in second gear due to excessive line pressure, the transmission shifted smoothly into third gear once Dylan loosened the kickdown linkage.
With the rally hood bolted down, Dylan McCool tackled the hour-long voyage home across four-lane highways and country back roads alike. Aided by its 2.76 rear gear ratio and tight steering, the 1972 Dodge Challenger cruised effortlessly between 60 mph and 65 mph. Aside from stiff rear air shocks and minor oil misting from the dipstick tube, the resurrected coupe completed the trip flawlessly.
